                                                       Chapter 1


Introduction

         Barangay governance in the Philippines depends on timely services and accurate

information, yet many barangays still rely on paper-based records and on announcements spread

by word of mouth. The need is greatest during floods, when residents must know which roads are

passable and which evacuation center is open. BARANGAYAN is a digital barangay

management system for Barangay Ampid I, San Mateo, Rizal that brings document requests,

incident reports, medical drives, and announcements into one system. Its main contribution is a

flood-weighted Dijkstra evacuation route with a separate Open-Meteo rainfall advisory. This

chapter presents the background, objectives, significance, scope, and delimitations of the study.


Background of the Study

         In the Philippines, the basic level of local governance is at the barangay, where the

smallest unit of administration can provide frontline services such as document processing,

incident response, and even community communication. Many of the Philippines' more than

42,000 barangays (42,004 as of March 31, 2024; Philippine Statistics Authority, 2024) still use

manual systems of paper-based process and face to face queues for barangay clearances,

certificates of indigency and residency certificates. Those with a need for these will often wait

for a long time, and there is seldom any clear sign as to how long it will take, if it will even get to

the right office for consideration. But not only that, barangays are also notified of what is

happening and what potential dangers are there in the area, such as flooding, damaged roads, and

illegal dumping. Usually these reports are recorded on paper, or shared informally through

messaging systems, making it difficult for barangay officials to remember which issue truly

requires their attention, or how they can prioritize issues for response  particularly during

emergencies like typhoons or the occasional flooding. If they don’t have a well organized, real

time reporting process, they simply can’t keep up with the demands of the community.

These constraints have been also reported elsewhere. Brillo et al. (2023) came up with

REPORTIT, a crime incident reporting and mapping system for Calamba. It did help with the

delays in police response, but this was limited in scope, to mainly crime related reports and

within the city. Barredo et al. (2023) built LBigayAksyon, an emergency response coordination

app for the Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office of Los Baños, Laguna.

Somewhat facilitated emergency response, but never really got to routine document processing.

Dela Peña (2025) studied an existing e-governance platform in Paracale, and found that, despite

its overall good performance, response time and software reusability continued to be areas of

weakness. Later, Webyu, a web-based barangay information management system for Barangay

Yuson and automated administrative workflows was introduced by Gasmido et al. (2025), but

mostly limited to records management for Barangay Yuson. Also it was not equipped with a

mobile application part. Combined, these studies highlight that the ongoing barangay-level

digitisation activity in the Philippines primarily addresses one of these functions, e.g., crime

reporting, emergency coordination, records keeping and/or general service delivery. None of

them combines these services with an evacuation route that avoids flooded and closed roads.

These problems are most serious during floods. When heavy rain comes, residents must know

which roads are still passable and which evacuation center is open, but this information is usually

spread only through announcements and word of mouth. Routing studies show that Dijkstra’s

algorithm can give a flood-aware route to the nearest shelter when flooded roads are given a

higher cost or removed (Piamonte et al., 2026; Ogawa et al., 2023), and open weather services

such as Open-Meteo give free hourly rainfall forecasts for any location (Zippenfenig, 2023).

These conditions illustrate the need for a digital barangay management system for Barangay

Ampid I that digitizes service requests and incident reports and, as its novelty, uses the flood

depths recorded by the barangay, the road closures of the Barangay DRRM and the blocked

roads reported by residents to recommend the safest route to an available evacuation center, with

an Open-Meteo rainfall advisory shown beside it. This need makes up the concept for

BARANGAYAN, a mobile and web-based digital barangay management system with

Dijkstra-based safest-path evacuation routing.


Project Objectives

     The main purpose of this study is to develop and test BARANGAYAN, a digital barangay

management system for Barangay Ampid I whose resident profiles, incident reports and DRRM

records feed one evacuation map. On this map, Dijkstra’s algorithm recommends the safest route

to the available evacuation center with the lowest flood-weighted route cost, and an Open-Meteo

rainfall advisory warns residents and officials when heavy rain is expected. In particular, the

study will:


    ●    Develop an evacuation routing module that uses Dijkstra’s algorithm to recommend the

         safest route from the resident’s location to the available evacuation center with the lowest

         flood-weighted route cost for walking, motorcycle or tricycle, or car, using the flood

         depths recorded by the barangay DRRM, the road closures it publishes, the availability of

         the centers and the roads reported as blocked by residents, with an hourly Open-Meteo

         rainfall advisory shown beside the route.

    ●    Develop the supporting barangay management features, namely resident profiles,

         document requests, medical drive registration and photo-based incident reporting, so that

         resident locations, reported incidents and DRRM updates feed the same evacuation map,

         with role-based access that supports the requirements of the Data Privacy Act of 2012

         (RA 10173).

    ●    Evaluate the application using ISO 25010 in terms of functional suitability, performance

         efficiency, compatibility, interaction capability, reliability, and security.

         Significance of the Study


         The study is significant to the following:

              ●    Barangay residents. Residents can request documents and barangay IDs online

                   instead of standing in line, which saves time and transportation expenses.

              ●    Barangay residents. Residents can report infrastructure damage or public

                   disturbances with photographic evidence and track the progress of document

                   requests and incident reports without visiting the barangay hall.

              ●    Barangay residents. Residents receive community announcements and emergency

                   messages on their mobile devices, together with a route to an available evacuation

                   center that avoids flooded and closed roads.

              ●    Barangay officials and administrators. The system gives staff a consolidated

                   online record store that reduces paper build-up, misplaced records, and manual

                   record keeping, and that supports the privacy requirements for personal

                   information.

              ●    Barangay officials and administrators. Automated request and incident-report

                   workflows reduce administrative time, and the incident map helps officials locate

                   problem areas and allocate resources.

              ●    Barangay DRRM and officials. Officials can publish road closures and

                   evacuation-center status that change residents' routes at once, and can use the

                   rainfall advisory and the evacuation map to decide where to send rescuers and

                   which roads to close.

              ●    Barangay communication. One broadcast channel allows timely announcements

                   and emergency instructions to reach the barangay at once.

              ●    Mobile computing and electronic governance. Existing systems such as

                   REPORTIT (Brillo et al., 2023), LBigayAksyon (Barredo et al., 2023), and

                   Webyu (Gasmido et al., 2025) handle crime reporting, emergency coordination, or

                   records, but none gives residents a route that avoids flooded and closed roads.

                   This study documents how an established algorithm and open weather data can be

                   applied to barangay disaster response.

              ●    Future researchers and developers. The study provides a documented reference

                   for applying configurable system design and known algorithms to local

                   governance in the Philippines, which can serve as a basis for future capstone

Scope and Delimitations


               Scope

         This study covers the design, development, and pilot evaluation of BARANGAYAN for

Barangay Ampid I, San Mateo, Rizal. It provides a resident Android application, a resident

website, and a staff and administrator website using React Native, Expo, Next.js, and Supabase.

Its main contribution combines flood-weighted Dijkstra evacuation routing with a separate

Open-Meteo rainfall advisory. Supporting modules cover profiles, document requests, payments,

incident reports, medical drives, announcements, and administration. Features are accepted only

after the specified tests pass; prototype screens alone do not establish completion.

         RESIDENT ANDROID APPLICATION

              ●    Digital Service and Document Request Module

                   Residents view document requirements, fees, and processing targets; submit

                   applications; and track pickup status. Profile records use separate first-name and

                   last-name fields. Residents submit identification and proof of residency for

                   authorized staff review; GPS is a preliminary check only. Household records

                   identify one designated household head for coordination. Relationship choices

                   depend on the selected member, and duplicate spouse links for the same person

                   are rejected. These rules remain subject to functional verification.

              ●    Automated Service Tracking Module (SLA)

                   Residents track document requests, incident reports, and health registrations

                   through their approved status stages. Processing targets identify overdue requests.

         Delimitations

             The study is confined as follows. Resident registration uses the device location only as a

preliminary check of whether the resident is inside Barangay Ampid I; it is not a requirement for

registration and is subject to the accuracy limitations of consumer GPS, so addresses outside the

barangay are reviewed manually by an administrator. The payment processing process

(PayMongo and QR Ph) is in sandbox or test mode during development and pilot testing, and

would need a separate account verification process with PayMongo for live or production

payment processing, which is not part of this study. The incident map and the evacuation-center

map are created using Leaflet.js and OpenStreetMap data, both of which are free to use for this

study and do not require a paid subscription or access key; a production deployment would need

a tile provider whose usage policy permits its traffic, because the public OpenStreetMap tile

servers allow only light use (OpenStreetMap Foundation, n.d.).

         Routing is limited to the mapped Ampid I network and the approved transport modes.

Recorded depths are historical inputs, not live street measurements. A missing depth is unknown;

the current zero fallback must not be presented as a confirmed dry road. Routes using incomplete

data require a visible limitation and DRRM review. No verified elevation model is assumed.

Synthetic networks and depths test the algorithm; they do not establish local flood accuracy.

Walking times use fixed speeds and exclude changes caused by rain, crowding, or floodwater.

         The advisory uses model-estimated rainfall and does not predict street flood depth or

river stage. Its thresholds require DRRM review and do not replace official warnings. Network

access is required for current weather, transactions, notifications, and shared updates. Only

stored guides and contacts may be read offline. The routing design excludes turn-by-turn voice

navigation, live tracking, and automatic destination switching; recalculation behavior must match

its test record. Android is the evaluated mobile platform. Pilot evaluation covers one partner

barangay and does not establish performance elsewhere.

                                                      Chapter 2


Theoretical Framework

         This chapter presents the routing model, rainfall advisory, supporting concepts, related

studies, and system architecture. The equations define how recorded road conditions affect route

cost, while the advisory communicates model-estimated rainfall separately.

         Dijkstra-Based Safest-Path Evacuation Routing with an Open-Meteo Rainfall Advisory

(Novelty of the Study)

         BARANGAYAN combines Dijkstra evacuation routing with an Open-Meteo rainfall

advisory for Barangay Ampid I. Routing selects the available center with the lowest

flood-weighted path cost for the chosen transport mode. Published closures, recorded depths,

blocked-road marks, and center availability determine the route. Rainfall estimates are displayed

separately and do not predict street flooding. The Historical Weather API supports test

preparation only. Related routing and warning studies inform this design; the study does not

claim worldwide priority or independently established forecast accuracy (Piamonte et al., 2026;

Ogawa et al., 2023; Young et al., 2021; Zippenfenig, 2023).


A. Road Network, Transportation Modes and Edge Weight of the Routing Model

         The road network of Ampid I is modeled as a weighted graph, G = (V, E), where V is the

G. Display of the Rainfall Advisory beside the Dijkstra Route in the BARANGAYAN


Mobile App

         The rainfall advisory and the Dijkstra route are shown together but kept separate in

computation. Open-Meteo returns one rainfall value for one grid cell that covers the whole

barangay, so any penalty built from it would give every segment the same factor c. The weight

would then become wm(e) = (1 + 10c) × d(e) for every segment, which multiplies the cost of

every path p by the same constant:

         cost'(p) = Σ (1 + 10c) · d(e) = (1 + 10c) × cost(p),   so the path with the least cost'(p) is

         the same path as the one with the least cost(p)

         Multiplying all costs by one constant cannot change which path is cheapest, so a rainfall

penalty would leave the route unchanged and only inflate the displayed costs, and removing

segments because of rainfall would remove all of them at once and leave every resident without a

route. For this reason rain never changes a route in BARANGAYAN: the route is decided by

Dijkstra, DRRM closures, center availability and the roads the resident marks as blocked, while

         In the BARANGAYAN mobile app, the server computes the level once for every

When the data is older than 3 hours or unavailable, the card states that rainfall information is not

ranking stay the same at every level, and the attribution "Weather data by Open-Meteo.com (CC

BY 4.0)" is shown with the card.

Electronic Governance and Digital Barangay Services

         E-governance is a term that refers to the practice of using technologies including

computers, mobile applications, and the Internet in order to provide services and keep records for

government organizations. E-governance makes it possible for government institutions to reach

out to residents without requiring their presence at government offices. As an example,

e-governance can be understood as a possibility of making a request in an electronic form, as

opposed to a paper one; electronically managing documents; and even keeping track of the stage

of the transaction with government organizations without having to come to the office in person.

         Barangayan, which can help one receive three types of documents from local barangays,

including good standing certification, certification of indigency, and proof of residency. Many

years ago, residents had to visit the local barangay office to fill in documents, wait in a queue to

submit their applications, and come back later to collect their documents. There were no ways of

knowing whether the applications were processed or not, not before visiting the office in person.

But now with the help of Barangayan, residents could apply with them knowing about their

applications.

         Dela Peña (2025) studied governance of a municipality in Paracale. He identified two

problems: delayed processing of requests and software that was hard to change once it was built.

Both problems matter for a barangay, where fees, requirements and processing targets change

over time.

         Barangayan addresses both of these issues. First, it introduces a tracking system which

describes every step that a request goes through, namely submission, review, approval or denial

as well as completion with a timestamp for each step. Both a resident and a barangay staff

member can know the current status of the request without being given any updates by others.

Second, the documents, fees and requirements of Barangay Ampid I are stored as data that the

barangay administrator can change, so the staff can add a document type or update a fee on their

own without a developer changing the code.

         Gasmido et al. (2025) explained the details of a barangay management system for a

specific barangay. The processing and language were done according to this barangay. Its

document types, fees and procedures were built around that barangay, and it has no mobile

application or disaster-response feature. Gasmido’s system allows setting up digitized records,

and workflows for one barangay whereas Barangayan builds on this for Barangay Ampid I by

letting the administrator change document types, fees and procedures without developer help,

and by linking these services to the evacuation map and the safest-route routing of the novelty.

         At the same time, all the studies focus on developing systems that improve how citizens

access barangay services but they vary in many crucial aspects. In the case of Dela Peña (2025),

it is evident that the study focused on a system implemented in a certain municipality and tested

its efficiency concerning getting access to barangay services and understanding what precise

aspects worked and what didn’t. Gasmido et al. (2025) researched a records and workflow

system for one barangay that does not include a mobile application or disaster-response features.

Community Incident Reporting and Geographic Information Systems

         Community incident reporting enables citizens to communicate local problems to

authorities. The problems may vary from non-functional streetlight, inundated road, garbage

which hasn’t been cleared or damaged pavement. Residents submit their complaint via direct

input into the system, thus eliminating the need to visit barangay hall or use the mobile app to

A Digital Barangay Management System with Dijkstra-Based Safest-Path Evacuation Routing and
an Open-Meteo Rainfall Advisory for Barangay Ampid I, San Mateo, Rizal
                                                                                                                           51


write a private message to the authorities. After entering the info into the system barangay staff

have an opportunity to react to complaints quickly.

         Geographic Information System, GIS, helps the authorities to enhance the system by

pinpointing the problem locations. When reports come along with geographical data, it makes it

possible for the authorities to see their problems on the map instead of going through hundreds of

complaints. This, in its turn, enables the authorities to determine the troublesome area. For

instance, when a number of complaints about flooding in the area appear , the officials

understand that it is necessary to solve the flooding problem instead of trying to deal with

random complaints.

         Brillo and colleagues, in (2023), created an Android app called REPORTIT that has a

web map paired with it. This app was produced to enable users to pass on incidents to the

authorities. Despite its efforts in the area of crime, the study did not ascertain whether this

procedure would be effective in other fields like road damage and pollution in the community.

On its part, the Barangayan app allows for different applications to be conducted including

infrastructure repairs, cleanliness activities and safety issues. All the reports are forwarded to a

particular barangay of the user rather than disseminated to the whole city that covers several

barangays.

         Barredo et al. in (2023) created another app called LBigayAksyon to facilitate the

operations of an office concerned in reducing the impact of disasters. The main aim of this

application was in creating connection and helping in coordinating needs of the citizenry with the

rescuers. The app was not able to perform the function of handling everyday issues like requests

for documents and handling paperwork. In this light, it can be seen that both apps have various

handling non-emergency issues.

         Inside the app a resident starts by filling out a form that asks for a title describing the

issue, a category selected from a list the current GPS location, a written description (optional)

and up to five photos. Before the report is accepted the system checks that all the details are

correct. It verifies that the latitude and longitude values are within real-world limits and that no

more than five pictures are attached. After validation the photos are uploaded to a storage service

and the report is saved as a new entry. Staff in the barangay can then access the data later.

         On the side barangay employees see all submitted reports displayed on an interactive

map. They can update the status of each report. Marking it as "under review " "in progress ".

Resolved”. As the problem gets worked on. This helps keep track of how fast issues are being

addressed.

         All three systems share an idea: turning a resident's observation into structured data so

local officials can take action. What sets Barangayan apart is that it is built around the needs of

Barangay Ampid I, where incident reports and blocked-road reports also feed the evacuation

routing. Whether combining incident reporting with functions actually leads to faster or

better-coordinated responses depends on real-world use. It cannot be decided by looking at the

code. The true test will come when residents and staff start using the system after it is fully

deployed.

Disaster Risk Reduction and Emergency Information

         A disaster risk reduction and management system is expected to accomplish several

things when disasters occur: warn people to take action; provide easy-to-understand visual

A Digital Barangay Management System with Dijkstra-Based Safest-Path Evacuation Routing and
an Open-Meteo Rainfall Advisory for Barangay Ampid I, San Mateo, Rizal
                                                                                                                         53


information about disaster; maintain an updated list of available safe shelters; communicate with

people to the safe shelters; and be aware of where people who may be affected by a disaster are.

The needs are the foundation of the Barangayan emergency module. It has various messages,

such as regular updates, important warnings, instructions for people to prepare for a disaster, a

list of evacuation centers, how to scan a QR code on arriving at a centre, and a way to check on

family members in an emergency. The concept of the module is to have the evacuation routing

novelty from the beginning of this framework, which is a Dijkstra-calculated safest route to the

available evacuation center with the lowest flood-weighted route cost for the chosen

transportation mode, displayed alongside an Open-Meteo rainfall advisory.

         This module shares similarities with LBigayAksyon (Barredo et al., 2023), as both are

concerned with ensuring the effectiveness of Emergency Response and reaching and

communicating to the people who need it. LBigayAksyon, however, coordinates reports between

residents and rescuers, and does not direct residents to an evacuation center. The evacuation

routing of Barangayan is similar to the map-based shelter guidance of Jeon et al. (2023) which

routes a user to the nearest shelter, or if a road is blocked to the next nearest shelter, and to the

evacuation operation management system of Jain et al. (2024) that assists residents in the

Philippines in finding an available evacuation center.

Medical and Vaccination Drive

         Vaccination and immunization management through digital means is an active priority in

the Philippines, recognized by the government. DigiVacc, a child immunisation system based on

the VaccTrace and VaccCheck Apps, was launched by the Department of Health, UNICEF

Philippines and the Government of Japan (2023). It was rolled out in 13 local government units

A Digital Barangay Management System with Dijkstra-Based Safest-Path Evacuation Routing and
an Open-Meteo Rainfall Advisory for Barangay Ampid I, San Mateo, Rizal
                                                                                                                         54


to link caregivers to health workers. Other factors that can impact uptake are self-registration and

scheduling tools, as demonstrated by Agarwal et al. (2022). Vaccination uptake at a primary care

clinic with a self-scheduling web and SMS platform was 51%, and 36-39% in the surrounding

town, county, and state, respectively. These studies collectively justify a system registering

residents and queuing them up, instead of one based on a purely walk-in basis.

         To allocate COVID-19 vaccines to Philippine communities, Culaste et al. (2023) created

a decision support system (DSS) that uses a weighted scoring based on an analytic hierarchy

process (AHP) and integer programming. They were able to operate under limited vaccine

supply and station capacity. If capacity was reached, it postponed the allocation of lower

priorities for the following day. The study demonstrates that a limited, limited supply can be

allocated in a workable manner through weighted prioritization.

         BARANGAYAN differs from these studies in three ways. DigiVacc is a national

immunization record system for children, and it is not used to share the limited stock among the

registrants during a single drive. At one clinic, Agarwal et al. (2022) conducted a study on

scheduling but did not assess the eligibility of registrants. Culaste et al. used weighted scoring at

the community level, solved using integer programming at several sites and days.

BARANGAYAN uses a resident-by-resident weighted scoring. It sorts residents by age, PWD

and comorbidity and it only employs a priority queue rather than the linear programming solve.

This is a lighter approach and is appropriate for a real time mobile environment within a single

barangay. It also shuffles no-show registrants' slots to the next-highest waitlisted resident, and it

keeps the numbers of remaining stock up-to-date.

Real-Time Information Management

         Real‑time information management means that a change made in one part of an

application appears immediately in another part without the user having to refresh or reopen the

app. For example when a barangay staff member confirms that a resident’s payment has gone

through that resident should see the updated status on their phone away rather than only finding

out the next time the resident opens the application. This capability is important in Barangayan

because many kinds of information the status of a service request the status of a payment updates

to an incident report information about a health drive and general barangay announcements all

must stay synchronized between what barangay office staff see and what appears on a resident’s

phone.

         The technology behind this feature is Supabase Realtime. Supabase Realtime allows the

application to subscribe to changes happening in parts of the database and push those changes

out to connected devices automatically. In practice the part of the application that tracks payment

status subscribes directly to changes on the underlying payments data so that a confirmed

payment is reflected on a resident’s screen as soon as it happens. As a safeguard against

situations where this live connection might be interrupted or delayed for instance because of a

mobile network, the same feature also periodically checks payment status through a separate

on‑demand request. This ensures that a resident is not left seeing information forever even if the

real‑time connection drops temporarily.

         The history of a service request’s status is kept through a shared tracking mechanism

paired with rules built directly into the database. These database rules automatically record a

status entry whenever a request changes state instead of relying only on the application’s

front‑end code to remember to log the change. This database‑level enforcement helps ensure that

A Digital Barangay Management System with Dijkstra-Based Safest-Path Evacuation Routing and
an Open-Meteo Rainfall Advisory for Barangay Ampid I, San Mateo, Rizal
                                                                                                                        56


the status history stays accurate and complete even if a particular screen or feature in the

application has a bug. Both the original design goal and the current implementation agree that

residents should see current status information at all times. What has not yet been established is

how quickly and how reliably an update actually reaches a resident’s screen under real‑world

conditions such as signal strength or high server load. That would need to be measured through

performance testing rather than assumed from the presence of these technical components alone.


Digital Payments and QR Ph

         Barangayans' way of collecting fees for barangay services depends on two parts:

PayMongo, a third-party service that handles payments and QR Ph, the national standard for

QR-code payments set by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. The BSP’s official memo on QR Ph

matters because it creates one government-mandated QR format that all banks and e-wallets

must support. Barangayan follows this standard of making its own custom QR code system.

         Inside the code all payment actions happen through server-side Edge Functions. These

functions run on the server not in the app itself. This means PayMongo’s private access key is

never stored inside the app, which keeps it safe from people who might try to look into the app’s

code. Five different Edge Functions manage payment tasks. One creates a payment when a

resident starts paying. Another checks if an existing payment has been completed or still

pending. A third cancels a payment if it’s no longer needed. A fourth issues refunds when

required. The fifth function receives and processes webhook messages from PayMongo; these

are notifications sent to confirm when a payment has actually gone through.

         The webhook function also checks a signature attached to each message. This step makes

sure only real messages from PayMongo are accepted. It stops someone from sending payment

an Open-Meteo Rainfall Advisory for Barangay Ampid I, San Mateo, Rizal
                                                                                                                         57


confirmed messages to trick the system. The function that checks payment status also verifies

that the person asking for information is the owner of that payment. This prevents residents from

seeing residents’ payment details.

         The system’s environment settings make it clear that using QR Ph properly needs setup

with a bank or licensed payment aggregator before any real money can move. Now the code

works in PayMongo’s sandbox mode, a test environment. It shows a separation between the

mobile app and PayMongo’s private keys, which is good security practice. Whether the payment

feature is truly ready to handle live transactions, with real money hasn’t been confirmed. That

would require finishing the settlement setup and testing everything in a production environment,

not just in the sandbox.


Privacy, Authentication, and Role-Based Access

         Barangayan handles data privacy using two main ideas. First role‑based access control

means a user can only see or do what their role allows. Second Republic Act No. 10173 The

Data Privacy Act of 2012 gives citizens clear rights over their own personal information. To

meet these rules Barangayan protects accounts, lets residents recover passwords, lets a resident

get a copy of their own stored data and lets a resident delete their account forever.

         Supabase Auth takes care of user authentication. On the app that residents use, the

resident’s session is saved on their own device. On the web‑based Admin Website a cookie keeps

the resident signed in. To decide if a resident can use admin features the system looks at the

resident’s role. Only an account assigned an administrator or staff position (Administrator,

Barangay Captain, Kagawad, SK Chairman, Secretary, Treasurer, Barangay Health Worker, or

A Digital Barangay Management System with Dijkstra-Based Safest-Path Evacuation Routing and
an Open-Meteo Rainfall Advisory for Barangay Ampid I, San Mateo, Rizal
                                                                                                                          58


Tanod) can reach those parts, and the position limits what the account may open. A regular

resident account is blocked from those parts no matter how the resident tries to get in.

         Two Edge Functions give residents the privacy rights that were mentioned. The first

function lets a resident download a copy of their own information, including the resident’s

profile, service requests, incident reports, health‑drive registrations evacuation‑center check‑in

records and device tokens. The function is built so that it only returns data that belongs to the

resident who asked for it. No one can pull another resident’s data. The second function deletes

any files the resident uploaded, cleans up the resident’s records from the database and finally

turns off the resident’s account using Supabase’s admin tools.

         These two functions match the privacy rights residents should enjoy, but having code for

export or deletion does not automatically make the whole system legal, under the Data Privacy

Act. Real compliance also needs Barangayan’s data‑retention policy: the consent forms residents

sign when they register and the internal steps Barangayan staff follow when they handle personal

data. None of these can be confirmed by looking at the application’s code.

through the running system, how the requirements were turned into the development build and

how the system is structured. The model shows the flow of Barangayan data, the model shows

architecture that structures the system.

Input–Process–Output Framework

         Barangayan's development uses an Input–Process–Output or IPO framework. The input,

process and output described here are about how data flows through the application when it is

running. This is different from the research approach shown in Figure 2.1, which outlines the

steps taken during the development phase to build the system. That earlier part focuses on what

was done not on the data the system handles.


Input

    ●    Registration and login details.

    ●    Resident profile and household-member information.

    ●    Document types, requirements, fees and target processing times set by the barangay

         administrator.

    ●    Service-request details and uploaded identification documents.

    ●    Incident category, description, GPS location and photographs.

    ●    Emergency announcements and preparedness content.

    ●    Evacuation-center details and QR check-in records.

    ●    Health-drive schedules, eligibility rules and stock counts.

    ●    Payment requests and PayMongo responses.

    ●    Administrative settings, staff accounts, FAQs and waste-collection schedules.

    ●    Routing inputs are the road graph, recorded flood depths, approved closures,

         blocked-road marks, and center availability. Open-Meteo rainfall is a separate advisory

         retain its source, issue date, scale, licence, and DRRM review status.

         Forms and server functions validate inputs before storage. For flood reports, the required

record fields are report ID, reporter role, road-segment ID, coordinates, reported time, depth in

metres or unknown, evidence, verification status, reviewer, review time, valid-until time, and

closure status. Unknown depth is stored distinctly from measured zero. Access and retention

follow the assigned role and approved policy.


System Process Flow

    ●    Checking the user's login session and role before each protected screen or action.

    ●    Validating form data on the client and against the shared schema helps keep data

         accurate.

    ●    Applying scoping and Row‑Level Security rules protects sensitive information.

    ●    Uploading photos and documents to Supabase Storage ensures that files are stored safely.

    ●    Writing, updating and triggering changes in the PostgreSQL database keeps the data

         current.

    ●    Sending real‑time updates to subscribed clients keeps everyone in sync.

    ●    Flood-data flow: resident or field staff report → DRRM verification → approved

         road-segment update → shared conditions → Dijkstra recalculation. Unverified reports

         remain labelled and must not be described as confirmed flood depth. DRRM reviews

         closures and expiry times before clearing a restriction.

    ●    Creating, checking and confirming PayMongo payments through Edge Functions secures

         the payment process.

    ●    Calculating service‑request status against processing-time targets shows whether each

         request is on time.

    ●    Recording administrative actions in an audit log provides accountability.

    ●    Running the data‑export and account‑deletion workflows, on request completes the

         cleanup process.

    ●    Computing the safest evacuation route for the chosen transportation mode with Dijkstra's

         algorithm (segment weight wm(e) = d(e) × (1 + 10 × fm(e))) and the rainfall advisory

         level (0 to 3) from the rain of the latest hour (R1) and the rain forecast for the next 3

         hours (F3).


Output

    ●    A catalog of the barangay services that residents can request.

    ●    Submitted service requests with their current status and status history.

    ●    Incident reports shown on a map for barangay staff and officials.

    ●    Emergency announcements and preparedness information screens.

    ●    Evacuation-center lists with occupancy status, and QR check-in records.

    ●    Health-drive registrations with their priority placement and status.

community's evacuation to the nearest shelters from water-level sensor data sourced from

PAGASA. BARANGAYAN adopts its edge weight w(e) = d(e) × (1 + 10f(e) + 0.5t(e)), where

f(e) is a flood-risk factor and t(e) is a traffic factor, with α = 10 and β = 0.5 set through testing,

but leaves out the traffic term because Ampid I has no traffic feed, which gives w(e) = d(e) × (1

+ 10f(e)). The same algorithm is used in the Dijkstra implementation over a road graph with a set

of evacuation centers, which is based on the heap. It is the most recent study in the Philippines to

Synthesis of Related Literature and Studies

         There are five main highlights of this review. The novelty of this study is the combination

of Dijkstra-based evacuation routing with the Open-Meteo Forecast and Historical Weather APIs

in a resident mobile application, a feature that has not been explored in other reviewed studies

that have been applied to flood settings (Piamonte et al., 2026; Ogawa et al., 2023; Jeon et al.,

2023; Young et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2026). Secondly, barangay e-governance systems can be

used to reduce delays stemming from paper based processes. The examples looked at here, Dela

Peña (2025) and Gasmido et al. (2025), were each created for one locality. Neither of them

connects barangay services to disaster response or evacuation routing.

Flood and road conditions reach the routing module through the following steps. Each step keeps

the record of who acted and when.


    1.   Report. A resident or authorized field staff submits a geolocated flood or blocked-road

         from a measured zero.

    6.   Expire. When the valid-until time passes, the record leaves the active set and stays in the

         archive. DRRM verifies the condition again if it continues.

Research Methodology

         The study uses developmental research to design, implement, and evaluate

BARANGAYAN, with Agile methodology guiding iterative software development. Functional

tests assess specified workflows, while task-based evaluation measures usability for the assigned

user groups. Planned functions, implemented features, and passed tests are reported separately.

         The proposed development plan consists of six four-week sprints within the six-month

work schedule. Each sprint repeats planning, design, development, testing, staging deployment,

and review; these activities overlap and are revisited as requirements and evidence change. Each

review demonstrates a working increment, records stakeholder feedback and defects, and updates

the backlog. A retrospective identifies improvements to the next sprint. Design covers the

three-tier architecture, database and access rules, interfaces, road graph, and per-mode routing

weights. Development integrates the Expo Android app, Next.js websites, Supabase services,

Dijkstra routing, and the separate Open-Meteo rainfall advisory. Testing includes workflow,

integration, access-control, hand-calculated Dijkstra, and injected-rainfall checks. Sprint

deployment uses test phones and a staging website with synthetic data and sandbox payments.

An increment is complete only when its agreed acceptance tests pass, critical defects are

resolved, and supporting records are updated. Final pilot evaluation retains the 50 planned

participants, role-based tasks, questionnaire, and DRRM simulated flood scenario; it does not

establish production readiness.

Verification of the Dijkstra algorithm

         The questionnaire in Table 17 measures how participants judge the screens and

workflows; it cannot show that the routing code computes the correct path. The correctness of

the Dijkstra implementation is therefore verified separately by comparing the route produced by

the app with a Dijkstra path calculated by hand on the same input. Dijkstra’s algorithm always

returns the least-cost path when no segment weight is negative, and every wm(e) in Equation 1 is

zero or positive, so a hand calculation that follows Equation 5 gives the correct answer that the

code must reproduce.

         For each test case, the researchers (1) draw a small road network of four to ten nodes with

known segment lengths, recorded depths, closures and evacuation centers; (2) compute every

segment weight with Equations 1 and 2 and work out Dijkstra step by step in a table like Table 5,

recording at every step the settled node, the tentative cost dist(v) of each node and the node it

was reached from; (3) read the hand-calculated route by following these nodes back from the

chosen center and compute its cost with Equation 4; (4) load the same network into the routing

function of the app through an automated test and record the returned route, the cost to every

center and the chosen center; and (5) compare the two results.

         The test cases cover each rule that can change a route: (a) the worked example of Tables

4 to 6 for walking, motorcycle or tricycle, and car, whose hand-calculated costs are already given

an Open-Meteo Rainfall Advisory for Barangay Ampid I, San Mateo, Rizal

in Table 6; (b) a segment on the recommended route that DRRM has closed; (c) a segment that a

resident has marked as blocked; (d) a recorded depth above the passability limit of one mode but

below the limit of another (Table 1), so the same network gives a different route for each mode;

(e) a nearer center that can only be reached through a flooded segment and a farther center that

can be reached through dry segments; (f) an evacuation center marked as unavailable; (g) a

network in which no center can be reached, where the app must report that no route is available

instead of drawing a path; and (h) two routes with exactly the same cost.

         A test case passes only when all of the following hold: the chosen evacuation center is the

same as in the hand calculation; the sequence of nodes of the route is the same as the

hand-calculated route; the cost to every center is equal to the hand-calculated cost when both are

rounded to one decimal place, as in Table 5; the cost of the route is equal to the sum of the

weights of its segments (Equation 4); and no closed, blocked or too-deep segment appears in the

route. When two routes have exactly the same cost, as in case (h), either route is accepted as long

as the cost matches. Each case is run again after a segment on the route is closed or flooded, and

the recalculated route of the app must again match the new hand-calculated route. Any mismatch

is recorded as a critical defect (Table 16), corrected, and the whole set of cases is run again.

         The results are reported per test case as the hand-calculated route and cost, the route and

cost returned by the app, and pass or fail. The evacuation routing is accepted only when every

The business model frames the market as three nested circles. The total addressable market

(TAM) is all 26,953 residents of Barangay Ampid I, the potential beneficiaries of barangay

services and evacuation information. The serviceable available market (SAM) is the residents

who have an Android device and internet access. The serviceable obtainable market (SOM) is

target will be set after the pilot validation.

payment-provider responsibilities, or legally required government procedures.

and receive the safest route to an available evacuation center in one app, while officials and the

DRRM manage requests, road closures and center status from one website.

risk. To mitigate against unauthorized access to data, the project utilizes role checks, row-level

security, storage policies, and access control testing. For payment or settlement yet to be put in

place, sandbox status is maintained until the service provider is verified and approved. To resolve

incomplete emergency information, the task of content review and updates is assigned to the

authorized staff of the barangay. Regarding interruption of provider or network, the system

provides error states, recovery methods, and alternative contact numbers of barangays. The

approved matrix for compatibility and accessibility should be tested before acceptance to handle

the limitations of devices, browsers, or accessibility. Geolocation is treated as a single check
